hints: Notice the question asks for potential difference between two points in a current-carrying wire where electrical energy is dissipated as heat.
Recall the defining relation $V = W/Q$ where $W$ is energy dissipated in $\text{J}$ and $Q$ is charge moved in $\text{C}$.
Connect power $P = W/t$ and current $I = Q/t$ to $W/Q$, and check which ratio gives units of $\text{J C}^{-1}$ or volts.
walkthrough: Start from the definition of potential difference: $V = W/Q$, the energy dissipated $W$ per unit charge $Q$ passing between the two points.
For a wire carrying current, write the rate relations: power dissipated $P = W/t$ and current $I = Q/t$.
The $1/t$ factors cancel, leaving energy per charge, so $P/I = V$. Unit check gives $\text{W A}^{-1} = \text{J s}^{-1}\text{A}^{-1} = \text{J C}^{-1} = \text{V}$.
Option A is field strength, option B gives $W/I$ and option D gives $P/Q$, neither of which simplifies to $W/Q$. The power to current ratio matches the definition. This is option C

options.A: Force per unit positive charge describes electric field strength $E$, not potential difference. Potential difference is energy per unit charge.
options.B: Energy dissipated divided by current gives $W/I$, which has units $\text{J A}^{-1}$ and not volts. It omits the rate at which charge flows.
options.C: Since $P = VI$, then $V = P/I$. Power dissipated divided by current equals energy per unit charge in volts.
options.D: Power divided by charge $P/Q$ has units $\text{W C}^{-1}$, not volts. Charge moved must be charge per unit time, which is current.
